subject: chemistry
promptStrong: Give me a challenging GCSE exam-style question on {lo}, then mark my answer against the AQA spec.
promptWeak: Explain {lo} for GCSE AQA Chemistry simply, with a worked example and the most common mistake.
learningObjectives: Extracting metals from ores (phytomining and bioleaching)
Reducing use of resources and recycling
Production and use of NPK fertilisers

questions.q: A finite resource is one that:
options: Is always made by living things
Is only found in the sea
Is being used up faster than it can be replaced
questions.explain: Finite resources (like crude oil and metal ores) are used up faster than they form, so they will eventually run out.

questions.q: Which of these is a renewable resource?
questions.explain: Timber is renewable because trees can be replanted and regrown. Crude oil, ores and natural gas are finite.

questions.q: Potable water is water that:
options: Is only obtained from the sea
Is completely pure with no dissolved substances
Is safe to drink, with low levels of dissolved salts and microbes
questions.explain: Potable water is safe to drink; it is not chemically pure but has low levels of dissolved salts and is free from harmful microbes.

questions.q: In the UK, fresh water is usually made potable by:
options: Filtering to remove solids, then sterilising to kill microbes
questions.explain: Fresh water is treated by passing it through filter beds to remove solids and then sterilising (with chlorine, ozone or UV) to kill microbes.

questions.q: Producing potable water from sea water by desalination is expensive mainly because:
options: Sea water has no salt to remove
Distillation or reverse osmosis needs large amounts of energy
questions.explain: Desalination (distillation or reverse osmosis) uses a lot of energy to remove the high levels of dissolved salts, making it costly.

questions.q: Sewage treatment includes which of these stages?
options: Screening, sedimentation, then aerobic and anaerobic biological treatment
questions.explain: Sewage is screened to remove grit, allowed to settle (sedimentation), then treated with aerobic bacteria for effluent and anaerobic bacteria for sludge.

questions.lo: Extracting metals from ores (phytomining and bioleaching)
questions.q: Phytomining extracts metals by:
options: Growing plants that absorb metal compounds, then burning them to form an ash rich in the metal
Using bacteria to produce leachate solutions
questions.explain: In phytomining, plants absorb metal compounds from low-grade ores; the plants are burned and the ash contains the metal compound.

questions.lo: Extracting metals from ores (phytomining and bioleaching)
questions.q: A key advantage of phytomining and bioleaching over traditional mining is that they:
options: Can extract metals from low-grade ores with less environmental damage
questions.explain: These biological methods let us extract metals from low-grade ores that were once uneconomic, with reduced environmental impact (though they are slow).

questions.q: A life cycle assessment (LCA) evaluates the environmental impact of a product across which stages?
options: Raw materials, manufacture, use, and disposal
questions.explain: An LCA considers extracting and processing raw materials, manufacturing, use, and disposal at the end of life.

questions.q: Why can parts of a life cycle assessment be difficult to compare objectively?
options: Assigning values to impacts like pollution involves judgement and can be biased
There are never any raw materials involved
questions.explain: Some effects (e.g. pollutant impact) are hard to measure precisely and require value judgements, so LCAs can be influenced by bias.

questions.lo: Reducing use of resources and recycling
questions.q: Which of these best reduces the demand on finite resources?
questions.explain: Reducing consumption, reusing items and recycling materials all cut the demand for limited raw materials and save energy.

questions.lo: Reducing use of resources and recycling
questions.q: Recycling metals is beneficial because it:
options: Always produces a purer metal than extraction
Uses less energy than extracting metal from ore and conserves the finite ore
Removes the need for any sorting
questions.explain: Recycling metals uses much less energy than mining and extracting from ore, and it conserves limited ore reserves.

questions.q: The rusting of iron requires the presence of:
questions.explain: Rusting is the corrosion of iron and needs both water and oxygen present; removing either prevents rust.

questions.q: Galvanising protects iron from rusting by coating it with zinc. This works because zinc:
options: Acts as a sacrificial metal, corroding in preference to the iron
questions.explain: Zinc is more reactive than iron, so it corrodes first (sacrificial protection) and also acts as a barrier layer.

questions.q: Alloys are often harder than pure metals because:
options: Different sized atoms distort the layers, making it harder for them to slide
They melt at a lower temperature
questions.explain: Adding atoms of a different size disrupts the regular layers of the metal, so the layers cannot slide over each other easily, making alloys harder.

questions.q: Which alloy is made mainly of iron with carbon and other metals, and resists corrosion?
questions.explain: Stainless steel is an iron alloy containing chromium and nickel; it is hard and resists corrosion. Bronze and brass are copper alloys.

questions.q: The Haber process makes ammonia from:
options: Nitrogen (from air) and hydrogen (from natural gas)
questions.explain: The Haber process reacts nitrogen (from the air) with hydrogen (mainly from natural gas): N2 + 3H2 reversibly forms 2NH3.

questions.q: The typical conditions for the Haber process are:
options: About 450 C, 200 atmospheres pressure, with an iron catalyst
questions.explain: The Haber process uses roughly 450 C, 200 atmospheres pressure and an iron catalyst as a compromise for a good rate and yield.

questions.lo: Production and use of NPK fertilisers
questions.q: NPK fertilisers provide plants with the elements:
options: Nitrogen, phosphorus and potassium plus carbon
questions.explain: NPK fertilisers supply the three main nutrients: nitrogen (N), phosphorus (P) and potassium (K).

questions.q: A composite material is made from:
options: Two or more materials combined to give improved properties, such as fibres in a matrix
questions.explain: A composite consists of a reinforcement (e.g. fibres or fragments) held together by a matrix (binder), combining useful properties of both.
